newsitem.title: CHINA: China's non-performing loans at 13-14 pct of total.
newsitem.headline: China's non-performing loans at 13-14 pct of total.

text.p: Non-performing loans now account for about 13 to 14 percent of total loans outstanding in China's banking system, central bank spokesman Ma Delun said on Wednesday.
About 2-3 percent of total loans were viewed as bad debts that would never be recovered, he told reporters.
"The ratio of non-performing loans to total loans is about 13-14 percent," he said.
"The money which can't be recalled is about 2-3 percent (of total loans)," Ma said.
The spokesman did not give specific figures for the total of non-performing loans and stressed that these statistics were estimates.
"We are still analysing the delayed payments to see how much can be recovered," he said, adding that authorities were trying to classify the types of non-performing loans.
China has been trying to shift its state-run banking system to shed its mantle of central planning and operate on commercial principles.
Under the old system, many state-run enterprises could count on credits from state banks and did not necessarily have to worry about repayment.

Many Chinese economists have long argued that the banking system was unfairly being called on to subsidise loss-making companies and that financial resources were being wasted on inefficient enterprises.

The central bank spokesman said the bulk of the non-performing loans were extended by the "Big Four" state banks -- the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, the Agricultural Bank of China, the Bank of China and the China Construction Bank.
These banks, with a longer history of operation, were often called on to make what officials call policy loans that supported industries considered to be important, regardless of their efficiency.
Ma said newer commercial banks had fewer problems and new loans extended by the banking system as a whole were now being made on commercial decisions.
"New lending policies are much more cautious," he said.
